Landlords and property managers need to keep property details, tenant information, and rent payments together. When these records are kept in notebooks or separate files, finding information and checking balances can take time. The Rental Management System was developed to bring these tasks into one desktop application.

The application uses Python and Tkinter for its screens and a MySQL-compatible database for storage. Its main sections are Dashboard, Properties, Tenants, Payments, and Settings. The current code supports adding and viewing properties and tenants, recording rent and balances, creating text receipts, saving settings, and logging out. Tenant records can also store paths to identification documents and LC1 letters.

Thirteen checks were run for this report on 12 November 2026. Ten checked source code and selected functions, and three checked logout using real Tkinter controls. All thirteen passed. Database calls were replaced during these checks, so the results do not confirm live database saving or physical printing. A database export is included in the project folder, but importing it and checking the full application remain separate tasks.

The project provides a useful starting point for managing rental records. The six main objectives are partly achieved. Editing, filtered search, complete lease tracking, detailed reports, and exports still need work. The login also needs stronger security, and payment history should be kept when a tenant or property is removed.

Managing rental property involves keeping details about houses or apartments, the people renting them, and the money paid each month. A manager may also need contact information, lease dates, identification documents, and receipts. These details are connected and should be easy to find.

Paper records and spreadsheets can work for a small number of tenants. As the number grows, it becomes harder to keep every record up to date. A payment may be recorded in one place while the tenant details are kept elsewhere. This creates extra work when checking an account or preparing a receipt.

The Rental Management System is a local desktop application intended for landlords and property managers. It brings property, tenant, and rent information into related screens. This report links the current application to the project proposal and the Phase 2 design.

Manual rental records can be misplaced, repeated, or entered incorrectly. A manager may find it difficult to confirm who occupies a unit, how much rent has been paid, or what balance remains. Separate files also make lease tracking and monthly reporting harder.

The project therefore aims to provide one place for rental records and routine payment work. The current application addresses registration and payment recording, while full lease management, search, and detailed reporting remain incomplete.

User action: enter the username and password, then sign in. Processing: the login page compares them with the demonstration values in config/settings.py. Result: the main layout opens when they match. An incorrect password is rejected and cleared. The current login is a demonstration check, not secure database authentication.

User action: choose Add Property and enter a name, location, number of units, monthly rent, and optional details. Processing: the form checks required entries and numeric values, then calls add_property(). Data: properties table. Result: the saved property appears when the table reloads.

Delete Selected asks for confirmation. The database function deletes payments linked through the property's tenants, then the tenants, and finally the property. It commits the changes together or rolls back if an error occurs. Property editing is not available.

User action: register a tenant and select an active property. Selecting the property fills its default rent, which can be changed for that tenant. The required details include the name, phone number, property, unit number, and rent.

Optional fields include email, lease start date, emergency contact, status, identification image path, LC1 letter path, and notes. The program stores document paths; it does not copy the documents into a managed folder. Deleting a tenant also deletes the tenant's payments. There is no tenant editing action.

User action: open Record Payment and select a tenant. The related property, unit, and rent are filled from that record. Enter the main amount, balance, payment date, method, reference, notes, and status. The program checks supported entries before saving.

The calculation is: amount paid = main amount - balance. For a main amount of UGX 500,000 and balance of UGX 150,000, the amount paid is UGX 350,000. The program rejects a negative balance, a balance above the main amount, and an invalid payment date. Status is chosen manually rather than calculated from the balance.
Cash, Mobile Money, Bank Transfer, and Card are record labels. Selecting one does not connect the application to a bank or payment gateway.

User action: select a saved payment and choose Print Receipt. Processing: the application creates a text file under data/receipts. The receipt includes company details, receipt number, tenant, property, unit, date, amounts, method, reference, and status.

On Windows, the program asks the default application to print the file. Creating the receipt file and successfully printing it are separate outcomes. Physical printing was not verified in the tests for this report.

The dashboard shows active property and tenant counts, unit totals, rent figures, occupancy, and recent activity. Current-month collected rent includes payments with status Paid. Pending rent is calculated as active tenants' expected rent minus that collected amount, with a minimum of zero.

Occupancy is estimated from active tenant count divided by total units. This assumes one active tenant record per occupied unit. It is not a separate unit-by-unit vacancy register. Manually selected payment statuses and duplicate tenant assignments can affect the figures.

Settings stores company and manager details, currency preference, rent due day, late fee, and reminder choices. Saving a reminder preference does not send an email or SMS. The late fee is not automatically charged. Several money displays still use UGX directly, even though a currency preference can be stored.

When the user chooses Logout, the application closes open forms, destroys the old pages, clears navigation references, and creates a fresh login screen. The password is cleared and must be entered again. Unsaved form entries are discarded, while saved database records are not deleted by logout.

Property forms check required details and whether units and rent can be converted to numbers. Tenant forms require the key details, check the selected property, and make a basic email check. Payment forms check the selected tenant, numeric amounts, date, and balance range. Settings checks the due day against 1 to 31 and requires a numeric late fee.

Examples of messages in the program include Missing Details, Invalid Amount, Invalid Balance, Invalid Date, and Database Error. These messages give the user a chance to correct an entry or check the database connection.

Some checks remain incomplete. Property and tenant rent need clearer non-negative limits. Phone format, document existence, duplicate unit assignments, and lease dates are not fully checked by the forms. A lost connection can also make some lists appear empty. Error reporting should be made consistent across all pages.

Database functions open a connection, run a query, and close the cursor and connection afterwards. Insert statements use parameter placeholders for record values. Successful writes are committed. Related deletions are rolled back if an error occurs. Settings uses an insert-or-update query to change existing values.

The design supports keeping saved data after the program closes because the records are stored in the database. A live save-and-reopen test is still required to confirm this on the target computer. Document files remain at their selected paths, while receipts are separate text files.

CHAPTER 5 - USER GUIDE AND PROJECT COMPLETION

The current application needs a Windows computer with Python and Tkinter, the mysql-connector-python package, and access to a running MySQL-compatible database. A default printer and an application that can print text files are needed for physical receipts. The project does not provide measured minimum processor, memory, or storage requirements.
1. Place the project folder on the computer. Open a terminal in that folder and install the application dependency:

2. Start the database server. In a database tool such as phpMyAdmin, create a separate database for the project and import rental_management_system.sql into it. The export contains both structure and existing records, so review it first and do not import it over a working database.

3. Check the connection settings in config/settings.py or set RMS_DB_HOST, RMS_DB_PORT, RMS_DB_USER, RMS_DB_PASSWORD, and RMS_DB_NAME in the environment. The default database name is rental_management_system. The program reads process environment variables; it does not automatically read a .env file.
4. Confirm that users, properties, tenants, payments, and app_settings can be read. Startup checks these tables but does not create them. Then run:
5. For the current classroom demonstration, the configured username is eric and the password is 12345. These fixed credentials should be replaced before use with real records.

6. Use sample data to check property entry, tenant registration, payment saving, and reopening the application. The supplied SQL export gives a setup starting point; a fresh import and complete live workflow were not tested for this report.
Sign in: open the application and enter the configured login details. The Dashboard opens after a successful login.
Add a property: open Properties, select Add Property, enter the property name, location, total units, and monthly rent, then save. Create the property before registering its tenants.

Register a tenant: open Tenants and select the registration action. Choose the property, enter the tenant name, contact, unit number, and agreed rent. Add optional lease and document details, then save. Keep selected document files at accessible paths.

Record rent: open Payments, choose Record Payment, and select a tenant. Check the property and unit, then enter the main amount, remaining balance, date, method, and other details. Use YYYY-MM-DD for the date. For rent of UGX 500,000 with UGX 150,000 remaining, the program records UGX 350,000 paid.
Create a receipt: select a payment and choose Print Receipt. Check the generated text file in data/receipts. If printing is needed, confirm that the default application and printer complete the job.
View summaries and settings: open Dashboard for totals and recent activity. Open Settings to change company details and available preferences. Reminder choices store preferences only.

Delete a record: select a property or tenant and confirm the deletion only when the linked records can also be removed. Deletion removes associated payments. Keep a database backup before trying this with records that matter.
Log out: choose Logout in the sidebar. Open forms close and unsaved entries are lost. The next user must sign in again. Saved records remain in the database.

The login uses fixed demonstration credentials and has no role-based permissions. Property and tenant editing, filtered search, complete lease tracking, move-out handling, tenant exports, and detailed financial and vacancy reports are missing.

Deleting a property or tenant removes related payment history. Units do not have their own records, and occupancy is estimated from tenant counts. Document paths can stop working if files are moved. Reminder preferences and late fees are not automated. Live database persistence and printing still need verification.

First, improve authentication and verify a repeatable database setup. Replace fixed credentials with securely stored passwords, use appropriate database permissions, and test the application against a separate database before introducing real records.

Second, finish property and tenant editing, filtered search, separate unit records, lease expiry, and move-out processing. Add checks for negative rent, duplicate active unit assignments, contact information, dates, and document paths.

Third, preserve historical records through archiving instead of deleting payments. Complete the approved financial and vacancy reports and export functions. Clearly distinguish stored reminder preferences from any future reminder service.

The Rental Management System brings property, tenant, and rent-payment records into one Python desktop application. Tkinter provides the screens, while a MySQL-compatible database stores the related records. The current code includes entry and viewing features, text receipts, a dashboard, settings, and logout.

All six main objectives are partly achieved. The system provides a base for routine rental records, but important parts of the approved plan remain incomplete. These include editing, search, lease management, full reports, secure login, and safe history retention. The thirteen passing checks support selected parts of the implementation; they do not establish full completion.

The project shows why related records need clear IDs and careful handling. A payment must match the correct tenant and property. Small calculation or input errors can affect rent figures, so validation should happen before saving.

It also shows that a feature in source code, a screenshot, and a successful live test provide different kinds of evidence. Testing needs to cover calculations, screen behaviour, database saving, reopening records, and output. Keeping interface, validation, and database responsibilities clear makes later changes easier.

The project is a useful desktop prototype for rental records. Completing the remaining features and carrying out live database and printer checks would make it more suitable for daily use. The next stage should focus on correctness, secure access, and keeping reliable payment history.
